strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First rigorous analysis of transfer learning with feature learning in both source and target tasks in infinite-width networks
Technically rigorous framework using statistical mechanics (replica trick, saddle point equations) with complete proofs
Excellent experimental validation: Theory predictions match DMFT simulations across linear, polynomial, and real datasets
Rich insights about transfer learning dynamics: reveals non-trivial trade-offs between elastic coupling, feature learning strength, and task similarity
Complementary theoretical perspectives: both Bayesian and gradient flow analyses provide independent validation
Clear presentation: well-organized despite technical complexity, with detailed appendices
Insightful phenomenology: identifies when transfer helps/hurts and mechanisms driving these effects
weaknesses: Restricted to two-layer networks: modern deep learning uses much deeper architectures; extension to depth unclear and severely limits practical relevance
Significant gap between theory and practice: elastic penalty δ||W - W̄||² is somewhat artificial; real transfer learning uses learning rate scheduling; mean-field parameterization not standard
Limited real-world experiments: only CIFAR-10 tested, only binary classification (2 classes per task); no experiments on standard transfer scenarios or with 10-way classification
No dataset averaging: theoretical equations scale with P₂, limiting predictive power for different dataset sizes; acknowledged limitation not addressed
Lack of practical guidance: no clear method to choose δ in practice; relationship to standard transfer learning hyperparameters unclear; no comparison with LoRA, adapters, or standard fine-tuning
Limited statistical rigor: missing error bars, confidence intervals, and significance tests on most experimental results; no ablation studies on key design choices
Incomplete technical justification: replica-symmetric ansatz assumed valid without rigorous justification; validity of mean-field limit for P₂ = O(N) not established
Methodology specificity: elastic coupling δ||W - W̄||² is one choice; alternatives not explored; only squared loss analyzed; sensitivity to architectural choices not studied

strengths: Novel theoretical framework combining feature learning with transfer learning in mean-field/μP infinite-width limit, extending prior work that recovers lazy kernels
Complementary analytical perspectives via both Bayesian (Result 1) and gradient flow (Result 2) frameworks with careful replica trick and DMFT derivations
Clear conceptual insights on elastic coupling parameter δ as control for feature reuse, interacting intuitively with feature learning strength γ₀ and task similarity
Rigorous mathematical exposition with graded experimental validation from linear networks with closed-form solutions through polynomial tasks to real datasets
Detailed appendices including replica symmetry analysis, saddle point equations, and special cases (linear networks, decoupled data, etc.)
weaknesses: Fundamental restriction to two-layer networks severely limits applicability; theory provides no insight into deep transfer learning (layer selection, hierarchy), modern architectures (ResNets, Transformers), or whether 2-layer insights scale
Non-standard transfer mechanism (elastic coupling δ||W−W̄||²) disconnects theory from practice where fine-tuning, layer freezing, and LoRA dominate; theory optimizes hyperparameter nobody tunes

Severely limited 'real' dataset experiments: grayscale 28×28 downsampled CIFAR-10, only 2-class source/target tasks, P₂=50 samples, MLP not CNN, no error bars/statistics, results only confirm intuitive predictions, missing standard baselines (pre-trained ResNets, realistic fine-tuning)

Finite-width experiments (N=20,000) lack convergence analysis or error bounds validating infinite-width asymptotics; theory assumes specific initialization, square loss, weight decay incomparable with modern practice
Unproven concentration assumption for free energy (Eq. 6) critical to theory; insufficient discussion of Replica Symmetry Breaking conditions and their implications for explored parameter regimes

Incremental novelty: Results 1 and 2 are extensions of recent work [14] and [26] with elastic coupling term added; unclear what fundamental insights emerge beyond adding δ||W−W̄||² to existing frameworks

Key experimental details (grayscale 28×28 CIFAR-10 preprocessing) relegated to appendices; figures lack quantitative error bounds and show only qualitative theory-simulation agreement; kernel visualizations difficult to interpret
Elastic coupling mechanism non-standard: practitioners don't optimize δ; creates disconnect where theory predicts optimal behavior under unused mechanism, limiting guidance for practitioners

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First rigorous analysis of transfer learning in the feature learning regime at infinite width (µP/mean-field scaling), advancing beyond prior work limited to NTK parameterization
Dual theoretical frameworks: Both Bayesian (aNBK) and gradient flow (DMFT) analyses are developed with consistent insights, providing robust understanding
Rigorous mathematical treatment: Careful derivations using replica trick, saddle point equations, and self-consistent solutions across different data regimes
Excellent theory-experiment agreement: Predictions match Langevin dynamics, gradient descent, and DMFT simulations convincingly across linear, polynomial, and real datasets

Mechanistic insights into transfer learning: Clear characterization of when transfer helps (task similarity, small datasets), role of elastic coupling δ vs feature learning strength γ₀, and task misalignment effects
Well-structured presentation: Clear motivation, intuitive explanations alongside formal results, systematic exploration of different regimes
Comprehensive appendix: Detailed mathematical derivations, multiple special cases (linear networks, same data, different labels), CNN extensions
weaknesses: Limited to two-layer networks: Significant restriction since modern transfer learning operates on deep networks where layer-specific decisions (freezing, fine-tuning) are crucial; extension to depth is non-trivial
Non-standard parameterization: Mean-field/µP scaling with specific learning rate η = η₀γ₀²N is not standard practice; connection to practical networks unclear and underdeveloped
Theoretical equations scale with dataset size: Saddle point equations scale with P, making theory cumbersome for large datasets compared to elegant scaling-law predictions in other frameworks

Elastic weight coupling is artificial: δ||W - W̄||² not standard in practice; no principled guidance for choosing δ; comparison to standard regularization (L2 on W, layer freezing, learning rate schedules) missing

Limited real dataset experiments: Only CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST on 2-layer MLPs with 2-class problems, downsampled grayscale images; no comparison to standard transfer learning methods or error bars
Incomplete practical guidance: No principled approach to hyperparameter selection (δ, β, λ, γ₀) in real applications; connection to practical fine-tuning deserves deeper treatment
Technical assumptions not fully justified: Replica symmetry ansatz assumed but not proven; convergence rate at finite width N not characterized; behavior as P/N varies not analyzed
Restricted scope of phenomena: No analysis of catastrophic forgetting, layer-wise transfer mechanisms, or relationship to other transfer principles; CNN section (D.1) underdeveloped

strengths: Develops novel theoretical framework for transfer learning in infinite-width networks with feature learning in both phases, extending prior work limited to fixed kernels or lazy learning
Comprehensive multi-scale analysis from general deep networks (Result 1) to explicit closed-form linear models (Results 2-4) with clear phase diagrams characterizing when transfer succeeds
Rigorous technical work: DMFT dynamics, path integral derivations, and careful limiting analysis appear sound; validated through Monte Carlo DMFT simulations and experiments

Clear interpretable insights: Results show how data quantity (ν₁, ν₂), task alignment (α), and feature learning strength (γ₁, γ₂) control transfer success; identifies regimes of positive transfer, negative transfer via noise crosstalk, and feature collapse
Exceptional technical depth: Thorough appendices with DMFT primer, detailed proofs, Bayesian extension, and multiple experimental settings (synthetic tasks, CIFAR-10, MNIST)
weaknesses: Severely limited practical applicability: infinite-width limit without finite-width error bounds, gradient flow instead of SGD, mean-field parameterization (µP) non-standard in practice, isotropic Gaussian data assumption; theory operates in regime distant from modern practice

Incomplete analysis of key results: Result 3 (finite-data effects) leaves coefficients c₁, c₂, c₃ implicit, only solved via DMFT saddle points (Appendix C.2); the ansatz (Eq. 11) is phenomenological, not rigorously derived. Deep networks beyond 2-layer lack detailed analysis

Restrictive assumptions throughout: all closed-form results assume isotropic covariance or linear/polynomial targets; real data structured; balance condition in Result 4 assumes specific initialization not discussed; random initialization arguments require large N without quantitative rates

Gap between theory and experiments: CIFAR-10 experiments use only 2 source + 2 target classes; ansatz for polynomial tasks (Fig. 2a) is phenomenological extrapolation, not rigorous. No standard baselines or comparison to existing transfer learning methods

Incremental methodological novelty: DMFT, path integrals, and Hubbard transforms are established; main novelty is application to transfer learning. Bayesian NN extension (Appendices E-F) uses different assumptions and feels disconnected

Dense presentation reducing accessibility: Results 1-4 stated formally without plain-language motivation; key derivations in appendix; connection between results and actionable insights unclear. Result 1 too complex for practical guidance; Results 2-4 restricted to linear models

Missing practical guidance: no recommendations for choosing γ₁, γ₂ beyond theoretical phase diagrams; no finite-width analysis to bridge theory-practice gap; no extension to CNNs, attention, or modern architectures; limited guidance on when theory applies

strengths: Technically rigorous DMFT-based framework with hierarchical analysis from general principles to explicit closed-form results for linear models

Interpretable theoretical insights about when transfer helps/hurts: data-rich pretraining improves transfer when aligned, finite-sample effects cause negative transfer, extreme feature learning limits transferability
Multiple levels of analysis (general framework, 2-layer networks, linear toy models, experiments) providing different perspectives
Consistent experimental validation showing good agreement between DMFT predictions and finite-width network simulations on synthetic tasks
Detailed mathematical derivations with extensive appendices supporting main claims
weaknesses: Limited practical relevance: infinite-width assumptions, isotropic Gaussian data, specific architectures don't capture realistic transfer learning (multi-layer freezing, diverse data, modern architectures)

Substantial theory-practice gap: CIFAR-10 results rely on ansatz for coefficients {c₁,c₂,c₃} inspired by extreme regime, making predictions post-hoc rather than predictive; kernel regression on fixed features differs from network dynamics

Incomplete deep network analysis: main results restricted to L=2 networks; for L>2 Appendix B states analysis is 'quite complex' with 'non-Markovian history dependence,' severely limiting applicability

Result 3 (finite-sample) validity concerns: adaptive kernel form (Eq. 11) relies on causal decomposition ansatz whose validity isn't rigorously justified; coefficients {c₁,c₂,c₃} left implicit, undermining predictiveness

Incremental theoretical contributions: DMFT for wide networks is established; adaptive kernels from feature learning studied in recent work; main novelty is applying existing tools to transfer learning setting
Presentation issues: dense notation (correlation/response functions, order parameters), overclaiming ('accurate predictions' when CIFAR results show partial agreement), unclear practical takeaways
Experimental limitations: small scale (CIFAR classes {1,2}→{8,9}, P₂=200), kernel regression on fixed features not equivalent to network dynamics, missing systematic ablations
Missing comparisons: no quantitative comparison with other transfer learning theories; position relative to concurrent work (Ingrosso et al., Tahir et al.) unclear

strengths: Novel theoretical framework for transfer learning in feature-learning regime (μP parameterization), filling gap between NTK lazy learning and practical deep learning
Rigorous DMFT analysis with multiple levels of detail: general dynamics, two-layer specialization, and closed-form linear models

Clear phase diagrams revealing when transfer helps: data-rich pretraining always helps (Result 2), finite samples cause negative transfer (Result 3), ultra-rich pretraining collapses features (Result 4)
Theory validated across synthetic tasks (linear/polynomial) and real datasets with consistent DMFT predictions matching finite-width experiments
Well-organized progression from general framework through tractable models, with interpretable conclusions on task alignment, data regimes, and feature learning strength
Mathematically sound: proper DMFT derivations, careful limiting time dynamics, correct saddle point equations and correlation functions
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: applies to infinite-width networks in μP parameterization with gradient flow, not finite-width networks with SGD in standard parameterization used in practice

Analysis largely restricted to two-layer networks; deep network case described as 'quite complex' with non-Markovian history dependence not fully characterized, limiting applicability to modern deep learning
Restrictive assumptions limit scope: isotropic Gaussian data, only regression tasks, MLPs only, proportional limit regime (P,D→∞ with P/D=ν fixed)

Experimental validation focused on synthetic tasks and limited real data (CIFAR-10 2-class subsets, image regression only); no systematic validation of finite-sample effects (Result 3) or comparisons with other transfer learning theories
Complex, non-intuitive results requiring solution of DMFT equations: Result 3 involves constants c₁,c₂,c₃ and loss expression (Eq. 13) with multiple terms whose practical implications are unclear
Key derivations and full analysis hidden in long appendices (C: 15+ pages, F: 10+ pages); main text relies on readers following extensive technical appendices

Some incremental aspects: task alignment helping is well-known; negative transfer with finite data noted before; novel contribution is quantitative characterization rather than qualitative phenomena discovery
Incomplete treatment of important questions: minimum width/samples for theory predictions, robustness to non-isotropic data, extension to standard parameterization, depth sensitivity
